items.title: Florida Evangelist Turning Defunct Vermont Campus Into ‘Christ-Centered University’
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: One evangelist from Florida is hoping to pick up where the Puritans left off in New England. Tommie Zito, an […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

One evangelist from Florida is hoping to pick up where the Puritans left off in New England.

Tommie Zito, an itinerant preacher who spends much of the year traveling internationally, has reportedly inked a deal with whiskey maven Raj Bhakta, who told CBN News in March he wanted to give away a $200 million college campus in Poultney, Vermont.

The founder of WhistlePig Whiskey had only one catch for his eyebrow-raising offer: the recipient of the sprawling campus — former home to the Methodist-affiliated Green Mountain College — needed to be a Christian who shared Bhakta’s view that biblical principles are vital to America’s flourishing.

“When we forget that there is a God above us who gives us the rules, we don’t make them — forgetting that is what has caused this crazy culture to emerge of hopelessness, and selfishness, and crazy ideas,” he said.

Zito hopes to turn the campus, a 26-building property with dorms, classrooms, athletic facilities, and more than 100 acres of farmland, into a “Christ-centered university” he’s planning to name “Z University,” according to the New York Post.

The Pentecostal preacher shared this video promoting the burgeoning project:

Zito plans for the Vermont campus to be the first of many faith-based educational hubs with additional campuses in Canada, Italy, Dubai, Poland, and Sri Lanka. Ultimately, he told the Post, he wants to add schools in Japan, Ireland, and the U.K., too.

“I’m sure it probably wasn’t their first choice to have a Christian university take over this beautiful campus,” Zito said of the local residents in Poultney, a town of roughly 3,000 people, according to census data from 2020. “Vermont and New England are not pro-church, let’s just say. We want them to know that I’m coming in here — we’re coming in here — to serve.”

As for Bhakta, he purchased the 115-acre property at auction for $4.5 million in 2020, following the Methodist school’s closure the year before.

While the whiskey mogul initially planned to give the property away, Zito said he “purchased it for a legit price,” but said Bhakta gave him a “fair” deal. Both Zito and Bhakta agreed not to disclose the purchase price at this time.

“It was a historic college and all we’re doing is taking it back, rebirthing it back, to its roots,” Zito said of his plans for the campus. “Ultimately, it’s going to be a blessing for Poultney, I really believe, and for the region.”

Calling the forthcoming college “an economic blessing,” he explained, “It’s going to bring life back — and not that there’s not life there right now, but there’s … definitely some areas around that, you know, could use some revitalization,” noting the school will offer education from “a Christ-centered, biblical worldview.”

Eventually, he wants Z University to function as a liberal arts college, offering training in evangelism, leadership, business, government, communication, and digital media that will be “heavy on the digital side … with AI.”

The minister said he plans for tuition to be comparable in price to other Christian colleges, like Grand Canyon University, which has a base tuition of $16,500 per year.

“I don’t do things to make money on it,” he told the Post. “We’re going to make it as affordable as we can. And that will depend on donor base, endowment, and all of that.”

Earlier this year, when asked how he’d define success for the Vermont property, Bhakta told CBN News “revival” is his goal.

“If we can plant a flag and bring a light to this place with an understanding of reorienting ourselves around God, family, and country, we can find purpose and bring the light, which was actually the motto of this campus when it began as a Methodist institution over 200 years ago,” he said.

The slogan Bhakta was referring to was Green Mountain College’s motto, Lux Fiat, which, in English, means “Let There Be Light.”

Bringing faith-based education to New England is far from a new idea — despite its now-post-Christian culture.

Ahead of America’s founding, the Puritan settlers in the Massachusetts Bay Colony and the Connecticut Colony, respectively, founded Harvard in 1636 and Yale in 1701 with the intention of educating the next generation of religious leaders in the region.

Z University — if it comes to pass — would mark a return of religious training to upper New England.

items.title: 5 of the World’s Most Dangerous Places for Christians: Shocking Persecution Stories
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "It is a stream of massacres..."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

As Christian persecution rages, Joel Veldkamp, head of international communications at Christian Solidarity International, continues sounding the alarm on the dire state of affairs.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Veldkamp recently appeared on the “Into the Supernatural” podcast to reveal five locations where he believes persecution has reached a fever pitch. The first nation he referenced is Nigeria, where he described a “slow-motion ethnic cleansing campaign.”

“There’s a region of the country called the Middle Belt, where most of the indigenous people who live there are Christians from hundreds of different people groups who are farmers,” he said.

“But there’s another tribe — a Muslim tribe called the Fulani — who are moving into this area, and they are extremely well-armed, and they formed a lot of militias, and, for the past eight years, really, they’ve been carrying out massacres of Christian villagers again, and again, and again on a weekly basis or more.”

Chaos in the region has led to a “slow expulsion of Christians,” with some recent events making international headlines. With each massacre, more and more believers leave the area.

“It is a stream of massacres, but it’s also a growing population of over a million people now who are just homeless, displaced, have no access to education or means of livelihood,” he said. “This is … probably the biggest persecution crisis in the world right now.”

Veldkamp also addressed other nations where persecution is raging, including Sudan, where he said there is a massive power struggle between “two Islamist factions” that used to run the nation together before turning on one another. The chaos has led to millions of deaths.

Sudan’s civil war broke out in April 2023 amid a struggle between the nation’s army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group. You can read more about that crisis here.

Veldkamp also spoke about Pakistan, Armenia, and Syria, addressing persecution issues unfolding inside these nations.

“Armenia … was a nation that converted to Christianity en masse in the year 301 AD,” she said. “And ever since then, its national identity, its culture has been intimately tied to Christianity.”

Veldkamp continued, “And this Christianity survived centuries of oppression by different empires, it survived the genocide of 1915, it survived 70 years of communist rule under communist Russia, and today, the genocide is continuing.”

He spoke about Azerbaijan targeting Armenia, as the mostly Christian-identifying population of Nagorno-Karabakh, a small landlocked region between the nations, was driven out.

“The entire population of this region called Nagorno-Karabakh, 120,000 people, had to flee from their lives to escape the … military advance,” Veldkamp said. “Today, the problem has kind of doubled in on itself because the Armenian government lost this war.”

He continued, “And when our government loses a war, you basically have two options, right? One is to say, ‘Sorry, everyone, we really screwed up. We’re going resign.’ The other is to say, ‘Actually, it was their fault,’ and that is what the Armenian government has decided to do. So they are blaming the refugees themselves for this problem, and they’re blaming the church in Armenia.”

Veldkamp said there are horrible issues now unfolding because of this, including arrests of faith leaders and other related problems. CSI has been in Armenia amid the troubling situation to support the refugees from Nagorno-Karabakh and make sure they have the resources that they need to preserve their community and their ability to advocate for themselves.

Meanwhile, Syria continues to face internal problems, with Veldkamp warning that Christians could face increasing problems.

“Syria is undergoing [a] slow Islamization process,” he said. “In other words, it’s becoming a lot more like Afghanistan than it used to be.”

The nation was ruled by a secular dictatorship until 2024, but recent developments have meant that the nation is now being led by Islamic leaders, with the new government headed by Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former al-Qaida member.

“This new president is really trying to show the international community, the West, that he’s a reasonable man, that he’s someone they can do business with, that they don’t have to be scared of him,” Veldkamp said. “Nevertheless, Syria is really going in the direction of major Islamization.”

Watch Veldkamp explain these issues among many others.

items.author: Leslie Koh

After hearing a talk
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Ben had bought pirated computer software for years, simply because it was cheaper. Even though it was illegal and broke copyright laws, he didn’t fell that it was morally wrong. After all, everyone did it, and why should he buy expensive original software? Who would check?

After hearing a talk on daily examples of living by God’s standards, however, Ben, a new believer growing in the faith, began to wonder, What does it mean to do the right thing?

Ben decided to replace all his software with original versions. It cost a lot more, but, as he explained to his friends, “God knows. And He calls us to do what’s right, right?”

In Amos 7, God reminded the Israelites that His standards were impartial and absolute. There was to be no compromise: they applied to all, including His favored nation. His laws and moral standards were like “a plumb line” (v. 8)—a weighted line used by builders to ensure structural integrity by showing if a wall wasn’t being built perfectly vertical.

While He may extend mercy, God can’t compromise His justice—which is why He sent His Son Jesus to die in our place as payment for our sin. The Bible shows us whether we’re walking in His way or not. By His grace, God helps those who believe in Jesus to live in a way that pleases Him and brings honor to Him—to do what’s right.

items.title: Pass It On
items.author: Sheridan Voysey
items.summary: After a fifty-five year wait, England’s soccer team finally made it to the European Football Championship Cup finals. Locked in a tie with Italy, the game was decided by a penalty shootout. England’s last chance fell to a young player named Bukayo Saka. But as Saka kicked the penalty sho
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

After a fifty-five year wait, England’s soccer team finally made it to the European Football Championship Cup finals. Locked in a tie with Italy, the game was decided by a penalty shootout. England’s last chance fell to a young player named Bukayo Saka. But as Saka kicked the penalty shot, Italy’s goalkeeper deflected it. England fans wept; the Cup was lost.

Few will forget what happened next, though. England’s manager, Gareth Southgate, walked over to the devastated Saka and embraced him. Southgate knew how Saka felt. In 1996 it was he, as a young player, who had missed the penalty shot that cost England a place in the semi-finals, and England’s then-manager Terry Venables had comforted him in the very same way.

“Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Paul says, “who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). Just as Southgate passed on to Saka what he’d received from Venables, Paul discovered that God’s comfort in his distress enabled him to comfort others in theirs, building their endurance (v. 6). Nothing is wasted with our “God of all comfort” (v. 3). He can use our disappointment for good.

One day Bukayo Saka will probably comfort a young player the way Southgate comforted him. Let’s do the same, passing on God’s comfort to create an endless chain of encouragement.

items.title: How Catholic Schools Can Cultivate the Sacramental Imagination
items.author: Dr. Ryan Messmore
items.summary:
Dr. Ryan Messmore

The sacramental imagination is a capacity for perception schools should cultivate by teaching students to see all things in the light of Christ.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Ryan Messmore

How do you teach someone to see differently? 

It is one thing to teach students a new subject like geometry or chemistry, but how can you teach them to look at a familiar subject—something already within their field of vision—and perceive deeper layers of meaning? How do you help someone move from sight to insight? 

In a previous article, I proposed that the lifeblood of teaching and learning in Catholic schools should be a way of seeing called the sacramental imagination. This is the human capacity to look beyond the surface appearance of everyday realities and recognize how they mediate God’s glory. Noting that it is more of a sensitivity than a skill, I argued that it can nevertheless be nurtured and developed. But how can people be led to see with new eyes? How can educators tune students’ imaginations to discern spiritual meaning in what they study? 

To help pupils see more of the “ten thousand places” in which Christ plays, Catholic schools would do well to focus on several key dispositions, skills, and practices within an intentional context.

Key Dispositions

To see the possibility of physical realities conveying divine self-communication, students must start with an authentic appreciation of the physical. Teachers should therefore look for ways to engage students in God’s material creation and make the truth being learned available to their senses. In short, get their bodies involved. Rather than only showing a photograph of a sunflower’s stamen or a caterpillar’s chrysalis, teachers should ask students to draw it. Rather than merely learning musical scales on paper, students should sing songs and play instruments. Rather than solely using a number line written on the board, educators should also teach students to count using pennies, blocks, or other manipulatives. Rather than just talking about astronomy, students should model celestial bodies with clay.  

Cultivating an appreciation for the physical also means exemplifying for students a genuine fascination with creation. Aristotle understood that knowledge begins with wonder. That’s easy to agree with, but how does an educator cultivate wonder or fascination in lethargic, distracted teenagers? The first step is to model it.

What prompts us to pay closer attention to something unknown: someone straightforwardly telling us that it’s necessary for good grades or someone excitedly asking, “Do you see that beautiful thing that I see?!” When students observe their teacher rejoicing in the elegance of a math equation or marveling at a caterpillar’s metamorphosis, they will likely be more disposed to approach their subjects with wonder, gratitude, and expectation. 

What, exactly, is the student expecting? That the object in question has something to communicate. In other words, creation speaks! One of the most important postures for Catholic school teachers to model, therefore, is expectant receptivity—a willingness to listen to and receive from their academic subject matter all that it has to disclose—and to respond in wonder. As philosopher Esther Meek put it, 

What starts the venture is notice and wonder. Something about reality catches our attention. To start to know is actually first a response to a dimly heard beckoning of the wonder-full real. If we can see knowing as a relationship between knower and known, we can see that reality makes the first overture. 

Providing students a daily witness of wonder, gratitude, and expectation is crucial for cultivating the sacramental imagination.

Another vital disposition for fostering an overture-and-response relationship with creation is what Michael Polanyi referred to as indwelling. By this, the brilliant twentieth-century scientist and philosopher meant a willingness not only to engage an academic subject with one’s whole person, including his body, but also to commit to it. (It is worth noting that “truth” and “troth” come from the same word. Students must betroth themselves—commit themselves with care and love—to what they want to know.) To indwell a discipline involves investing it with one’s time, attention, sympathy, and trust, and then seeing where it leads. Sometimes the fruit of imaginative seeing only comes through giving oneself first to a mystery and following where its surprising possibilities point. This is another posture that teachers can best encourage within students by modeling it themselves.  

Key Skills

One of the most important skills employed by the sacramental imagination is that of attending to an object closely. Students cannot hope to discern an invisible truth unless they look carefully at what mediates it. One good way to train this sort of attention is to ask students to keep a nature journal in which they record with words and sketches what they observe in the natural world. Another valuable method is to have students look closely at a beautiful painting and describe all the details they see. It is amazing what we can perceive when we just slow down and take the time to notice what is in front of us. Effective teachers do just that.

Order Your Set Today

Nature journaling and picture studies engage students in the sort of expectant receptivity mentioned above—what philosopher Simone Weil called “waiting without searching.” This entails bringing to an object an open mind ready to see something new. Rather than assuming he knows what a chrysalis looks like because of a photograph in his textbook, an attentive student suspends prior judgment, sits before an actual chrysalis, and gazes at it with fresh eyes. Being asked to draw a detailed sketch in a nature journal can facilitate this sort of attention, thereby increasing the student’s aptitude for grasping truth. And even though the truth of a chrysalis is a “little fragment of a particular truth,” it is, according to Weil, “a pure image of the unique, eternal and living Truth . . . [who] once in a human voice declared ‘I am the Truth.’” In this way, Weil maintains that every school exercise is like a sacrament.

Another helpful skill for tuning the imagination is asking questions about the object to which one attends. This should flow naturally from the sense of wonder, curiosity, and receptivity mentioned above, but teachers can prime the pump by asking their own questions. As my friend and educator DeAnn Stuart proposes, such questions include “What do you notice?”; “Did anything surprise or startle you?”; “Why do you think it works that way?”; and “What do you think God is trying to communicate to us?” 

Furthermore, asking students if they detect any patterns or likenesses with other things they have seen—or if it reminds them of anything else they have read or experienced—can also help cultivate their sacramental imagination. For example, a theology teacher who knows that his colleague is discussing caterpillar metamorphosis in science class can ask students how that knowledge might shed light on certain New Testament passages. After all, a form of the Greek verb metamorphoō is used to describe not only Jesus’s transfiguration (Matt 17:2, Mark 9:2) but also the transformation his disciples are called to undergo through the renewing of their minds (Rom 12:2). Integrating knowledge across disciplines is a key skill for honing the sacramental imagination.

Practices 

Not surprisingly, the most powerful practice for cultivating this capacity is participation in the sacraments of the Church. A school that celebrates the Eucharist together frequently predisposes its students to discern hints of God’s presence in other physical objects around them.

Teachers can also enhance their students’ imaginations by providing them a stockpile of beautiful images, artistic compositions, and compelling stories. As I noted in my previous article, we interpret the meaning of something by finding a place for it to fit within the interpretive grid—that web of interconnected images, concepts, and experiences—that is present in our minds and memories. Therefore, placing before students beautiful objects to behold, compelling characters to identify with, and meaningful events to remember thickens that web and increases their ability to find related meaning in what they study.   

And the stockpile of images for a Catholic student should be amply furnished by Scripture. But trained educators should do more than merely encourage Bible reading; they should assist students in reading the Bible typologically. Guided by the Church’s interpretive tradition, this way of attending to Scripture can help students make appropriate connections between the Old and New Testaments. Coming to perceive Jesus as a new Temple, how the Passover lamb prefigures the sacrifice of the cross, and what Peter meant by speaking of Noah’s ark as a figure of Christian baptism (1 Pet 3:20–21) can help students see beyond the surface level of objects and events.

A Context of Comprehensive Faith 

Finally, if the sacramental imagination is a capacity for perception, schools should cultivate it by teaching students to see all things in the light of Christ. But simply offering theology courses is not enough. Such a limited approach would be like looking at a beam of light in a dark room in hopes of seeing a caterpillar that it shines upon. Rather, as C. S. Lewis argued, it is more illuminative to look along the beam, which entails stepping into its path and turning to see what it enlightens. For students to learn to view their academic subjects in the light of Christ, Catholic schools must invite them to step actively into his light. 

This means providing a comprehensive environment marked by faith, from the policies in the handbook to the paintings on the wall to the PE teachers in the gym. Students need to sense that the Catholic faith is relevant not just to a private corner called “religion class” or “chapel time” but to all of life. As Lewis also asserted, “I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen: not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.” The full curriculum is illumined by the light of Christ, and the entire school provides an interpretive grid for grasping the meaning of life in him. 

Conclusion

The sacramental imagination is not the academic product of a single unit plan, nor can it be developed by a plug-and-play procedure. Instead, it is a sensitivity that is nurtured within a certain kind of culture and by teachers genuinely curious about the deeper dimensions of their field. From this vantage point, Christ’s light can illumine the deeper meaning of realities all around us, including the lifespan of a single butterfly. Cultivating the sacramental imagination can therefore open up to students vistas not discernible by physical eyesight. In the words of the French novelist Marcel Proust, “The real voyage of discovery consists not in seeking new landscapes, but in having new eyes.”

items.title: WOF 540 | How the Virtues Help Us Respond to an Increasingly Vicious Online Culture
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Is it still possible to make evangelical headway in this increasingly noxious online environment? If so, what principles should guide the way?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Welcome back to the Word on Fire Show. I’m Matthew Petrusek, senior director of the Word on Fire Institute and the host of the Word on Fire Show. Thank you for joining us. From Bishop Barron’s very first social media post close to 20 years ago, he and Word on Fire as a whole have recognized that the online world is a rough-and-tumble place. While most, over the years, have interacted with our content with charity and respect, even if they disagree, there’s always been a gallery of trolls who traffic in insults and profanity and are only interested in taking potshots at the ministry rather than engaging in conversation. So it goes—that’s just part of the price of entry into the digital world, especially when evangelization is your goal.

The internet culture, however, seems to have taken a dark turn recently. Whatever limited restraint people used to show in their online interactions seems to have evaporated in a toxic cloud of mob-fueling—and mob-fueled—rage, replete with distortions, deceptions, and sometimes even explicit calls for violence. Exacerbated by the rise of the use of AI, bots, and anonymous accounts often based in foreign countries, it is increasingly difficult to know with whom you are engaging online or what their motives are. And sadly, physical threats from online sources are now also something we must take very seriously. So how should we move forward from here? Is it still possible to make evangelical headway in this increasingly noxious online environment? If so, what principles should guide the way? Here to discuss the challenges and possible solutions to the current state of the online world is Bishop Robert Barron.
